reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ATS-ERS
clinicalPearls: A small-airways disease in which fibrosis narrows and obliterates the bronchioles, producing largely irreversible airflow obstruction (constrictive bronchiolitis)
This obliterative form should be distinguished from bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia, which is a different, steroid-responsive process
Presents with progressive breathlessness and dry cough, often with a surprisingly clear chest radiograph relative to the degree of impairment

Important causes include lung and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (chronic rejection/graft-versus-host disease), connective tissue disease, prior infection, and toxic inhalational exposures such as diacetyl in flavourings
After lung transplantation the clinical entity of progressive obstruction is termed bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome and is a leading cause of late graft failure
Expiratory high-resolution CT shows mosaic attenuation with air trapping, reflecting patchy small-airways obstruction
Pulmonary function testing shows fixed airflow obstruction with air trapping that responds poorly to bronchodilators
Management focuses on treating any underlying cause, removing exposures, and immunomodulation in transplant-related disease, since established fibrotic obstruction is largely irreversible
reference.pathophysiology: Constrictive bronchiolitis obliterans is caused by inflammation and concentric submucosal and peribronchiolar fibrosis of the membranous and respiratory bronchioles, progressively narrowing and ultimately obliterating their lumens. The insult may be immune-mediated (chronic rejection after lung transplant, graft-versus-host disease, connective tissue disease), post-infectious, or toxic from inhaled chemicals. The resulting patchy small-airways obstruction produces air trapping and mosaic perfusion, while the larger airways and alveolar architecture are relatively preserved, which is why chest radiographs can appear near normal. Once fibrosis is established the airflow limitation is fixed.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and emphysema
Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (distinct entity despite the shared historical name)
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis with a bronchiolar pattern
additionalInvestigations: Pulmonary function testing demonstrating fixed airflow obstruction with air trapping
Inspiratory and expiratory high-resolution CT to show mosaic attenuation and air trapping
History of transplantation, connective tissue disease, infection, or inhalational exposure
Surgical lung biopsy where the diagnosis remains uncertain, since changes can be patchy
Post-transplant monitoring of spirometry to detect bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome early
redFlags: Rapidly declining spirometry after lung or stem cell transplantation indicating progressive graft dysfunction
Recent high-intensity toxic inhalational exposure with acute symptoms
reference.prognosis: Because the airway fibrosis is largely irreversible, the natural history is one of stepwise or progressive decline; outcomes depend on the cause, and post-transplant bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome in particular is a major limitation on long-term graft and patient survival.
pitfalls: Confusing constrictive bronchiolitis with the steroid-responsive organizing pneumonia that shares part of its historical name
Being falsely reassured by a near-normal chest radiograph
Missing air trapping by omitting expiratory CT images
Overlooking an occupational inhalational cause such as flavouring chemicals
